title: Friction: the grip that works against sliding

summary.text: Friction is the grip between two surfaces that touch, and it always works against sliding. It is why your chappal does not slip on the road, and why a rolling ball slows down and stops. Friction also turns movement into heat and slowly wears things away. Rough surfaces, rubber and pressing harder give more friction, while oil, water and wheels give less. Scientists can measure friction well, but they still argue about exactly why surfaces grip, and even why ice is slippery.
summary.art: A split picture: on the left a child's shoe gripping a stone step (tiny zigzag bumps meeting under a magnifying glass); on the right the same shoe sliding on wet ice, arms flailing.

intro.hook: Try this. Hold a pencil between two fingers, as lightly as you can. Now imagine your fingers and the pencil were perfectly slippery, like wet soap. Could you still write your name?
intro.text: Nearly four thousand years ago, workers in Egypt moved a huge stone statue across the desert. It was about as heavy as ten elephants. They dragged it on a wooden sledge, a big flat sled with no wheels. An old wall painting shows the scene. At the front, one man is doing something strange. He is pouring water onto the sand. Why would he do that? By the end of this unit, you will know. It has to do with friction, the grip between things that touch.
intro.art: The tomb painting idea: rows of men pulling ropes, a giant statue on a sledge, one small figure at the front pouring water from a jar onto the sand.

outcomes: I can say what friction is: a force where two things touch, which works against sliding.
I can run a fair test to find out which surface grips best, changing only one thing at a time.
I can read a forcemeter or a ruler to compare friction, and show my results in a table and a bar chart.
I can give examples of where we want more friction and where we want less, and say how people change it.
I can explain that friction turns movement into heat and slowly wears things away.
I can say what scientists agree about friction, and what they still do not know.

I can explain that friction comes from tiny atoms pushing and pulling on each other. I can also give big examples: tides slowing the Earth, slippery knee joints, and a super-cold liquid with no friction at all.

terms.meaning: A push or a pull. Forces make things start moving, stop, speed up, slow down or turn.
terms.example: You push a door to open it. A magnet pulls a pin towards it.
terms.art: Two arrows: one hand pushing a door, a magnet pulling a pin.

terms.meaning: The outside of a thing. It is the part that touches other things.
terms.example: The bottom of your shoe is a surface. So is the top of the floor.
terms.art: A shoe sole and a floor, with the touching parts glowing.

terms.meaning: The grip between two things that touch. Friction always works against sliding.
terms.example: Your chappal grips the road, so you don't slip when you walk.
terms.art: A shoe on the ground with a small arrow at the sole pointing against the way it wants to slide.

terms.meaning: When two surfaces hold on to each other well. Lots of friction means good grip.
terms.example: Rubber soles grip a wet bathroom floor better than smooth plastic soles.
terms.art: A rubber sole with deep grooves holding on to a wet tile.

terms.meaning: When one thing moves across another while still touching it.
terms.example: A book sliding across a table. A child going down a playground slide.
terms.art: A book with motion lines sliding on a table.

terms.meaning: When a round thing turns over and over as it moves. Only a tiny part of it touches the ground at any moment.
terms.example: A ball rolls. A wheel rolls. Rolling a heavy thing is much easier than dragging it.
terms.art: A wheel with one small contact point marked.

terms.meaning: The grip that stops a thing from starting to slide. It is usually a little stronger than the grip once the thing is moving. Scientists call it static friction.
terms.example: A heavy almirah is hardest to move at the very first push.
terms.art: A child straining at a box that hasn't moved yet.

terms.meaning: The grip on a thing that is already sliding. It is usually a little weaker than starting friction.
terms.example: Once the almirah starts moving, it is a bit easier to keep pushing.
terms.art: The same box now moving, the child pushing more easily.

terms.meaning: Something slippery put between two surfaces to make the friction smaller. Oil, water, soap and powder are lubricants.
terms.example: Oil on a squeaky door hinge. Powder on a carrom board.
terms.art: A carrom board with a sprinkle of powder and a striker gliding.

terms.meaning: A surface with bumps you can feel or see.
terms.example: Sandpaper, a coconut shell and a stony road are all rough.
terms.art: A magnified rough surface like mountains.

terms.meaning: A surface whose bumps are too tiny to feel. Under a microscope, even smooth things are bumpy.
terms.example: Glass and a polished marble floor feel smooth.
terms.art: Polished glass, and the same glass under a microscope showing tiny hills.

terms.meaning: A tool that measures how strong a pull is. Inside it is a spring. The harder you pull, the more the spring stretches, and a pointer moves along a scale of numbers.
terms.example: Hook a forcemeter to a shoe and pull the shoe along the floor. The number shows how much friction you are pulling against.
terms.art: A spring forcemeter hooked to a shoe, the pointer at 3 N.

terms.meaning: The unit for measuring force, just as the centimetre is a unit for length. It is named after the scientist Isaac Newton. The short way to write it is N.
terms.example: Holding up a small apple takes a force of about 1 newton.
terms.art: A hand holding an apple, '1 N' written beside it.

terms.meaning: When two things rub together, some of their movement turns into warmth.
terms.example: Rub your palms together fast. They get warm.
terms.art: Two rubbing hands with little heat squiggles.

terms.meaning: Friction very slowly rubbing tiny bits off a surface.
terms.example: Old temple steps have a dip in the middle. Millions of feet rubbed the stone away over hundreds of years.
terms.art: Ancient stone steps with a dip worn in the centre.

terms.meaning: The pattern of grooves on a tyre or a shoe sole. It helps them grip, and lets water escape on wet ground.
terms.example: New bicycle tyres have deep tread. Old tyres worn smooth are called bald, and they slip more easily.
terms.art: A new tyre with deep tread next to a bald tyre.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope. One grain of sand has more atoms in it than there are grains of sand on all of India's beaches.
terms.example: Your shoe, the floor and the air are all made of atoms.
terms.art: A zoom from a shoe to a speck of rubber to a cluster of tiny balls.

terms.meaning: An even tinier particle on the outside of every atom. Electrons carry electric charge, so they push and pull on each other. When two surfaces touch, it is really their electrons pushing and tugging.
terms.example: Friction, the floor holding you up, and a rubbed balloon sticking to a wall all come from electric pushes and pulls.
terms.art: Two atoms side by side with clouds of electrons at their edges, nudging each other.

terms.meaning: What it takes to make something move, warm up or change. Energy never disappears. It only changes from one kind into another.
terms.example: A rolling ball has movement energy. When friction stops the ball, that energy becomes a tiny bit of heat.
terms.art: A ball rolling, then stopped, with warm squiggles where its movement went.

terms.meaning: A very strange liquid that flows with no friction at all. Scientists make it by cooling helium, a gas, until it is almost as cold as anything can ever be.
terms.example: Superfluid helium can creep up the inside wall of its cup, over the rim, and drip off the outside.
terms.art: A glass cup with a thin glowing film of liquid climbing up the inside and dripping off the bottom outside.

terms.meaning: The sea rising and falling, about twice a day. It happens mainly because the Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans.
terms.example: At Mumbai's beaches, you can walk far out on the sand at low tide.
terms.art: A beach at high and low tide, the Moon above.

explanations.definition: Friction is a force that acts where two surfaces touch. It works against sliding, or against something starting to slide.
explanations.description: Friction only appears when two things touch and one of them is sliding, or is being pushed or pulled to slide. It always acts against the sliding. Think of a book lying still on a flat table. Nobody is pushing it, so there is no friction on it at all. Now give the book a gentle push. Friction pushes back the opposite way, and the book soon stops.
examples: A ball rolling on grass slows down and stops. The grass rubs against it.
When you walk, your foot pushes back on the ground. Friction pushes your foot forward, so you move ahead.
A bicycle brake rubs against the wheel. The rubbing slows the wheel down.
explanations.art: Three panels: ball slowing on grass, foot pushing back on ground with a forward arrow, a brake pad on a wheel.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what friction is.

explanations.description: Everyone agrees on what friction does. The harder question is why two surfaces grip each other at all. Over the centuries, scientists have given different answers. The study of friction even has its own name: tribology. At the level of atoms, the full story is still being worked out.
examples: Sandpaper grips wood because its sharp bumps catch on the wood.
In space, two very flat, very clean pieces of metal can stick together when they touch. Scientists call this cold welding.

perspectives.who: Leonardo da Vinci, an Italian artist and inventor, around 1493, and Guillaume Amontons, a French scientist, in 1699
perspectives.explanation: Every surface is covered in tiny bumps, even if it feels smooth. When two surfaces touch, the bumps catch on each other, like the teeth of two combs pushed together. To slide, the bumps must climb up over each other.

perspectives.who: John Desaguliers, a scientist in London, in 1734
perspectives.explanation: Surfaces stick because their tiny particles pull on each other. He pressed two very smooth lead balls together, and they stuck. So smoother does not always mean more slippery.

Both ideas are partly right. Two surfaces really touch only at the tips of their tiny bumps. At those tips, atoms of one surface stick to atoms of the other. As the surfaces slide, those little joins are torn apart again and again. Exactly how this happens is still being studied.

explanations.art: Two magnified surfaces like mountain ranges touching at a few peaks; at one peak, a close-up of atoms holding hands across the gap.
explanations.context: Scientists agree on what friction does. This card is about why it happens, which has had different answers over 500 years.

explanations.concept: Starting is harder than keeping going
explanations.definition: It is harder to start something sliding than to keep it sliding. The grip that stops things starting is called static friction. Once a thing is sliding, the grip is a little weaker. That weaker grip is called sliding friction.
explanations.description: When two surfaces rest together, their tiny bumps settle into each other, and more of their atoms stick. So at the start, you have to pull hard to break them free. Once the thing is sliding, the bumps have no time to settle. So the grip drops a little, and pulling gets easier. The graph shows this. A forcemeter, a spring tool that measures pulls, is pulling a shoe across the floor. The pull rises while the shoe stays still. The moment the shoe starts to slide, the pull drops. Then it stays about the same.
examples: Pushing a heavy box: the very first shove is the hardest. After that it gets a little easier.
Pull a shoe with a forcemeter. The number climbs, then drops back a little the moment the shoe starts to slide.
explanations.art: A forcemeter reading 5 N as the shoe starts, then 3 N as it slides.
explanations.context: Have you noticed that the first push on a heavy box is the hardest? This card explains why, with a graph of a shoe being pulled.

chart.title: Pulling a shoe across the floor (a made-up example)
chart.note: The shoe stays still until 5 seconds, then starts to slide. The pull drops from 5 newtons to 3 newtons.

explanations.definition: Friction depends mainly on two things. First, what the two surfaces are made of. Second, how hard they are pressed together.
explanations.description: Rubber on stone grips much more than plastic on ice. That is the first thing: the materials. Pressing harder also gives more friction. A full bag presses on the floor harder than an empty one, so it is harder to drag. Here is the surprise. For hard things like bricks and wooden blocks, the size of the touching part hardly matters. A brick slides about as easily on its big flat side as on its thin edge. The pictures show made-up readings for a brick pulled both ways. People were puzzled by this for hundreds of years. The rule does not work for soft, sticky things like rubber tyres or sticky tape.
examples: An empty school bag is easier to drag than a full one.
A brick lying flat and the same brick standing on its edge need about the same pull.
Racing cars use wide, soft tyres. For soft rubber, more touching area does give more grip.
explanations.art: A brick lying flat and on its edge, each pulled by a forcemeter showing the same number.
explanations.context: Why is one thing easy to drag and another hard? This card names the two things that matter most, and one surprise about bricks.

show.caption: Brick on its thin edge: also 6 newtons

explanations.definition: Rolling and lubricants both make friction smaller. A lubricant is something slippery, like oil, water, soap or powder, put between two surfaces.
explanations.description: A wheel does not scrape along the ground. As it rolls, each part touches the ground and then lifts off again. So there is very little rubbing. A lubricant works in a different way. It makes a thin, slippery layer between two surfaces. The layer keeps them a little apart, so their tiny bumps do not catch as much.
examples: Round logs or rollers under a heavy stone make it far easier to move.
Oil on a bullock cart's axle, the rod the wheel turns on, helps the wheel spin.
Powder on a carrom board lets the striker glide.
explanations.art: A heavy stone on log rollers; a carrom striker gliding on powder.
explanations.context: People have always looked for ways to make heavy things easier to move. This card explains the two big tricks: rolling, and slippery layers.

explanations.concept: Friction makes heat and wears things
explanations.definition: When surfaces rub, some of the movement turns into heat. Tiny bits of the surfaces also get rubbed off. This rubbing away is called wear.
explanations.description: The movement does not vanish when a thing stops. It turns into a little warmth in the surfaces and in the air around them. Rubbing also scrapes off tiny bits, far too small to see one at a time. Over a long time, this wears away even stone.
examples: Rub your hands together fast and they get warm.
A match lights because rubbing it on the box makes its tip very hot.
Brake pads, shoe soles and the tips of erasers slowly get used up.
explanations.art: A match head striking a box with a spark; an eraser shrinking over a week.
explanations.context: When something rubs and stops, where does its movement go? This card explains that it turns into warmth, and that rubbing also wears things away.

explanations.description: You might think scientists worked this out long ago. They have not. There are a few main ideas, and scientists still argue about which ones matter most.
examples: Ice skates glide easily over ice.
Very cold ice, at about 30 degrees below zero, is less slippery than ice that is close to melting.

perspectives.explanation: The weight of a skate presses on the ice and melts it into water. Most scientists now think this pressure is far too weak to explain it, except perhaps under thin skate blades.

perspectives.who: Michael Faraday, an English scientist, in 1850, and many scientists today
perspectives.explanation: Ice always has a very thin, almost wet layer on its surface, even when nothing presses on it. That layer is slippery.

Sliding itself makes heat, and the heat melts a thin film of water. Some recent experiments also suggest the top layer of ice molecules can roll and tumble like tiny marbles. The full answer is still open.

explanations.art: A skater on ice; a magnifier showing the top layer of ice molecules looking loose and wobbly.
explanations.context: Ice is slippery. Everyone knows that. This card is about a surprise: scientists still do not fully agree on why.

explanations.concept: Friction is really electricity between atoms
explanations.definition: All friction comes from electric pushes and pulls between the atoms of two surfaces. Scientists call this the electromagnetic force.
explanations.description: Zoom in to where two surfaces touch, and keep zooming. You reach atoms. The outer parts of atoms are electrons, which carry electric charge. Electrons of the two surfaces push each other away. Atoms of the two surfaces also tug on each other and hold on for a moment. Sliding means breaking those little holds again and again. This same electric force makes the floor push up on you, so you don't sink into it. It also makes a rubbed balloon stick to a wall. Gravity pulls you down. Electric forces between atoms hold you up and give you grip.
examples: The floor holding you up and your shoe gripping the floor are the same kind of force.
Press two thin fridge magnets face to face and slide one. You feel a clicky, sticky slide. It is a giant model of atoms attracting each other and letting go.
explanations.art: A zoom in four steps: a shoe on a floor; bumps touching; atoms at one bump; electron clouds pushing and tugging, labelled 'electric force'.
explanations.context: This card zooms in, far past anything a microscope can show. It finds out what friction really is, deep down.

explanations.concept: Where the movement goes: jiggling atoms, and the arrow of time
explanations.description: Heat is really atoms jiggling. Think of a box sliding across the floor. All its atoms move together, neatly, in one direction. Friction takes that neat movement and spreads it out. It becomes the messy jiggling of countless atoms in the box and the floor. That is easy to do, and almost impossible to undo. A warm floor never pushes a box back across the room by itself. Physicists agree on this rule. They call it the second law of thermodynamics. Many think it is also why time only seems to go one way, forwards. That bigger idea is still argued about.
examples: Film a box sliding to a stop, then play it backwards. It looks wrong straight away.
Stir milk into tea. It never un-mixes by itself.

perspectives.explanation: Time seems to go one way because things always spread from neat order into mess. Friction is one of the ways that happens.
That explains which way things change. It does not explain what time itself is. That question is still open.

explanations.art: A box sliding and stopping, then a 'rewind' panel with a red cross: the floor can't push it back.
explanations.context: This card follows the movement that friction takes away. It links it to one of the biggest questions in science: why time only goes forwards.

explanations.definition: A superfluid is a liquid that flows with no friction at all. Scientists make one by cooling helium to about 271 degrees below zero.
explanations.description: That is colder than anywhere in nature on Earth, and close to the coldest anything can ever be. At this cold, the strange rules of quantum physics show up at a size we can see. Quantum physics is the science of the very tiniest things. The helium atoms stop acting like separate little balls. They move together, like one single wave. Because the atoms move as one, there is nothing inside the liquid to rub. So the liquid can flow through gaps far too tiny for water. It can climb up the walls of its cup. Once stirred, it keeps swirling without slowing down. It was discovered in 1937 and 1938. Pyotr Kapitsa found it in Moscow. John Allen and Don Misener found it separately in Cambridge, England.
examples: Stir a superfluid and it keeps going round and round without slowing.
It creeps up and over the rim of its cup as a very thin layer.
explanations.art: A cup of glowing superfluid helium with a thin film climbing over the edge, and a little swirl that never stops.
explanations.context: Is there anything with no friction at all? This card is about a real liquid that has none.

explanations.concept: Friction from empty space: quantum friction
explanations.description: Quantum physics is the science of the very tiniest things. It says empty space is never perfectly empty. It fizzes with tiny flickers of energy. Some physicists have worked out what this means for sliding. One of the first was John Pendry, in 1997. Two perfectly smooth surfaces sliding past each other, very close but not touching, should still feel a tiny drag. The drag would come through those flickers. Other physicists have argued about whether this really happens. Nobody has measured it yet. Experiments are being planned to test it.
examples: Imagine two plates sliding past each other a hair's width apart, never touching, with no air between them.

perspectives.who: John Pendry, a British physicist, and others
perspectives.explanation: It should exist, but it is far too small to notice in everyday life.
Some ways of calculating it are wrong. The real drag might be zero, or different from what was predicted.

explanations.art: Two plates gliding past each other with a tiny gap, the gap filled with faint sparkles labelled 'empty space is not empty'.
explanations.context: This card is about a friction that scientists predict but have never measured. It is a tiny drag between two things that never touch.

explanations.concept: Tidal friction is slowing the Earth
explanations.definition: Tides are the sea rising and falling, about twice a day. As tides move over the sea floor, friction slowly brakes the Earth's spin. So each day is getting very slightly longer.
explanations.description: The Moon's gravity pulls the oceans into a bulge. The spinning Earth drags that bulge along, and the water rubs against the sea floor. This friction takes away a little of the Earth's spin. Because of it, a day gets about 2 thousandths of a second longer every 100 years. That is far too small to notice. But over hundreds of millions of years, it adds up. Corals that lived 400 million years ago grew one thin line each day. They grew about 400 lines a year. So a year then had about 400 days, and each day lasted only about 22 hours. Some of Earth's spin is passed on to the Moon. The Moon drifts about 3.8 centimetres further away every year. Scientists measure this by bouncing lasers off mirrors that astronauts left on the Moon.
examples: About 400 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs, a day lasted about 22 hours.
The Moon moves away from us about as fast as your fingernails grow.
explanations.art: The Earth spinning with ocean bulges, a brake-pad icon on the sea floor, the Moon a little further away each frame.
explanations.context: Friction is not only small. This card shows how friction from the sea is slowly making Earth's days longer, and pushing the Moon away.

chart.title: How long one day lasted, then and now

explanations.description: Living things are very good at controlling friction. Your knee joints rub every time you move, for your whole life. The ends of the bones are covered in smooth, soft cartilage, soaked in slippery joint fluid. Together they slide with less friction than ice sliding on ice. Gecko and tree-frog feet can grip and let go in a moment. And what about the ridges on your fingertips, your fingerprints? People used to say they help us grip. A 2009 experiment found that on smooth, dry surfaces, they do not.
examples: Knees, hips and finger joints move millions of times, for many years, before they wear.
A gecko, a small lizard, can run straight up a glass window.

perspectives.explanation: Fingerprint ridges help us grip, like the tread on a tyre.

perspectives.who: Peter Warman and Roland Ennos, two scientists in England, in 2009
perspectives.explanation: They tested fingers on smooth, dry surfaces. The ridges actually lowered the grip a little, because less skin touched the surface.
Ridges may help on wet or rough surfaces, by letting water escape. They may also mainly help us feel textures, because they vibrate as we touch things. The question is still open.

explanations.art: A magnified fingertip with ridges touching glass at a few lines; a knee joint with cartilage and fluid glowing; a gecko on a window.
explanations.context: Your body is full of parts that rub against each other. This card looks at how living things control friction, and at a surprise about fingerprints.

agreed.text: Friction acts where two surfaces touch, and it works against sliding.
agreed.evidence: On Earth, every sliding thing slows down unless something keeps pushing it. In space, with nothing to rub on, a pushed thing keeps moving.

agreed.text: Friction depends on what the surfaces are made of, and on how hard they press together.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have measured this carefully since 1699, when a French scientist, Guillaume Amontons, did careful tests. Children repeat these tests in classrooms every day.

agreed.text: It is usually harder to start something sliding than to keep it sliding.
agreed.evidence: Pull a shoe with a forcemeter, a spring tool that measures pulls. The number climbs until the shoe starts to slide, then drops a little.

agreed.text: Friction turns movement into heat, and slowly wears surfaces away.
agreed.evidence: Rubbed surfaces get warm. Brake pads, shoe soles and stone steps wear away over time.

agreed.text: Friction costs the world a lot of energy.
agreed.evidence: In 2017, two engineers, Kenneth Holmberg and Ali Erdemir, added up the friction and wear in the world's machines. They estimated it uses up about 23 out of every 100 units of energy people use. That is nearly a quarter.

chart.title: Of all the energy people use, how much is lost to friction and wear (an estimate)
chart.unit: out of every 100 units of energy

data.label: Lost to friction and wear: 23 out of 100

challenging.claim: Moving things stop by themselves, because stopping is natural.
challenging.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker who lived about 2,350 years ago. Most of us also think this without noticing.
challenging.for: It matches what we see every day. Balls, carts and bicycles all stop if nobody keeps pushing them.
challenging.against: About 400 years ago, Galileo, an Italian scientist, noticed something. The smoother the surface, the further a ball rolls. So things stop because friction and air slow them down. In space, a pushed ball would keep going for ever.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of how things move, and why scientists gave it up.

challenging.claim: Friction is a nuisance, and we should get rid of it.
challenging.who: A common way of thinking, especially about machines
challenging.for: Friction wastes energy. It wears out engines, shoes and roads.
challenging.against: With no friction at all, you could not walk or hold your food. Knots would come undone. You could not light a match, stop a bicycle or play a violin. You would even slide off your chair. We need the right amount of friction, in the right places.
challenging.context: This card looks at a common view of friction: that it is only a problem.

challenging.claim: Guillaume Amontons discovered the rules of friction, in 1699.
challenging.for: Amontons, a French scientist, published the rules in 1699. Science usually gives the credit to whoever publishes first.
challenging.against: Leonardo da Vinci, the Italian artist and inventor, wrote the same rules in his notebooks about 200 years earlier. But his notebooks were not published, so his work was forgotten for centuries.
challenging.context: This card is about who gets the credit for discovering the rules of friction.

challenging.claim: In the old Egyptian painting, the man pours water on the sand only as a religious ritual, not for any practical reason.
challenging.who: Some experts on ancient Egypt, in the past
challenging.for: Pouring water was part of religious ceremonies in ancient Egypt.
challenging.against: In 2014, scientists in Amsterdam tested this with a small sledge on trays of sand. The right amount of water roughly halved the pull needed. So the workers seem to have known something useful. Scientists only explained it about 3,900 years later.
challenging.context: About 3,900 years ago, Egyptians painted workers dragging a giant statue on a wooden sledge. One man pours water on the sand. This card asks why.

challenging.claim: Ice is slippery because pressure melts it.
challenging.for: Very strong pressure can make ice melt at a slightly lower temperature.
challenging.against: The pressure from a shoe is far too small to melt ice. Yet ice is slippery even when you are standing still on it.
challenging.context: This card is about an old explanation for slippery ice that is still found in some books.

challenging.claim: Meteors and returning spacecraft get hot because of air friction.
challenging.for: They get extremely hot while racing through the air. And rubbing makes heat.
challenging.against: Most of the heat comes from squashing the air in front of them. They push into it so fast that the air heats up enormously. A bicycle pump gets warm in the same way when you squash air in it, but far less. Rubbing against the air plays a much smaller part.
challenging.context: Meteors are space rocks that burn up as they fall through the air. This card is about why they, and spacecraft coming home, get so hot.

big_questions.q: If you rolled a marble in empty space, would it ever stop? And why does everything on Earth stop?
big_questions.hint: On Earth, the marble rubs against the ground and the air. What is there to rub against in space?

big_questions.q: When a rolling ball stops, where has its movement gone?
big_questions.hint: Rub your hands together fast. What do you feel?

big_questions.q: Is there anything in the world with no friction at all?
big_questions.hint: Scientists have made a very strange, very cold liquid that has none. Why do you think zero friction is so rare?

big_questions.q: Would a world without friction be better or worse? What would you miss first?
big_questions.hint: Imagine breakfast, the walk to the park, writing your name, and giving someone a hug.

big_questions.q: Friction slows things down. But it also pushes us forward when we walk. Can one thing both help us and get in our way?
big_questions.hint: Can you think of other things in life that are both?

big_questions.q: A chappal grips a dry floor but slips on a wet one. So is the grip in the chappal, in the floor, or in between?
big_questions.hint: Try the same chappal on two different floors. Then try two different chappals on the same floor.

big_questions.q: In this unit's story, workers in ancient Egypt drag a giant statue across the sand. The strong pullers seem to do the real work. The man pouring water on the sand is laughed at, yet his small job is what lets the statue move. Who gets remembered for big achievements, and who gets forgotten?
big_questions.hint: Who 'poured the water' in your family or school today? Whose small job made everything easier?

big_questions.q: Friction turns a sliding box's movement into jiggling atoms, and it never turns back. Could that be why we remember yesterday, but not tomorrow?
big_questions.hint: Watch a video of a ball rolling to a stop, played backwards. Why does it look wrong?

big_questions.q: Your knees rub every time you move, for eighty years or more. How might a body make something more slippery than ice?
big_questions.hint: Think about the smooth, soft layer on the ends of the bones, and the slippery fluid between them.

big_questions.q: Scientists think even 'empty' space might cause a tiny friction. So is anything truly empty?
big_questions.hint: Hold your hands close together without touching. What do you think is in the gap?

big_questions.q: Friction from the sea is slowly making days longer and pushing the Moon away. Is anything in the universe permanent?
big_questions.hint: About 400 million years ago, a day lasted about 22 hours. Will people one day have 25-hour days?

story.title: The Water-Pourer
story.note: The tomb painting is real, and so is the 2014 sand experiment in Amsterdam. Mery, Hapu and what happened to them are made up.
text: Nearly four thousand years ago, at the edge of the desert in Egypt, a stone giant lay on its back. It was a statue of a governor called Djehutihotep. It had been carved from a single block of stone. It was taller than four men standing on each other's shoulders, and as heavy as ten elephants. It lay on a wooden sledge, a big flat sled with no wheels. Between the giant and the river lay a whole day of sand.

Mery was ten years old, and she had not been chosen to pull. The pullers were the strong ones. There were more than a hundred and seventy of them, in four long lines. Each man had a rope over his shoulder and his toes dug into the sand. Mery's job was to carry jars of water from the river to her father, Hapu. And Hapu's job, the whole of it, was to walk at the very front of the sledge and pour water onto the sand.

The pullers laughed at him. 'Look, Hapu is watering the desert!' they called. 'Will you grow us some cucumbers, Hapu?' Hapu only smiled and kept pouring. He did not pour a flood, and he did not pour a trickle. He poured a steady curl of water that turned the pale sand just a little darker, the colour of a ripe date. Mery noticed that he never let it turn to mud. When the water made a puddle, he waited. When the sand dried, he poured again.

On the first day, the giant moved. The foreman, the man in charge, beat the rhythm on a drum. The men leaned and heaved together. The sledge slid forward, one long breath at a time, across the darkened sand.
That night, Hapu shook with fever. In the morning, he could not stand. 'No matter,' said the foreman. 'Pouring water is not real work. Today the men will just pull harder.'

So they pulled harder. The drum beat. The ropes creaked. The sledge did not move. Its front edge pressed into the dry sand and pushed up a little hill in front of it, like a cow trying to walk through a heap of grain. The harder the men pulled, the deeper the sledge dug in. One rope snapped with a crack like a whip, and three men tumbled into each other. Someone muttered that the statue was cursed.

Mery stood holding her jar, her heart thumping. The jar was heavy, she was only ten, and nobody had asked her anything. But she had watched her father for a whole day. She walked to the front of the sledge, past the men glaring at her, and she poured.
She poured too much. The sand turned to mud, the front of the sledge sank into it, and the men groaned. 'Get away, child,' the foreman snapped.

Mery's face burned. She stepped back. She looked at the mud, and at the dry sand beside it, and she remembered the colour of a ripe date. Not too wet. Not too dry. She moved a little to one side and tipped the jar gently. She drew a steady curl of water across the sand, just enough to darken it. She waited. She poured again.

The sand changed under her feet. When it was dry, it had shifted and slid away like sugar. Now it held together, firm as a path. No little hill rose in front of the sledge. 'Pull,' whispered Mery. Then, louder: 'Pull now!'
The drum beat. The men leaned. And the stone giant, as heavy as ten elephants, slid forward over a thin skin of darkened sand, as smoothly as a fish through a river.

All that day, Mery walked at the front, pouring and waiting and pouring. The giant followed her like a patient animal. Nobody laughed. Late in the afternoon, one of the pullers came over to her. It was the man who had joked about cucumbers. He took her empty jar, carried it to the river, and filled it for her.

When the statue was finally standing, the governor's painters painted the whole journey on the wall of his tomb. They painted the giant on its sledge, the four long lines of pullers, the drummers and the foreman. And at the very front, so small that you could miss him, they painted a single figure pouring water from a jar onto the sand.

Nobody wrote down Hapu's name, or Mery's. But somebody painted them. And nearly four thousand years later, in a laboratory in Amsterdam, scientists pulled a tiny sledge across trays of sand. Some trays were dry, some were damp and some were soaked. They measured what a water-pourer at the edge of the desert had known all along.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the statue does not move because people pull harder. It moves because the surface where sledge meets sand changes. Dry sand piles up in front of the sledge and holds it back. Just-damp sand holds together, so the sledge slides over it. Too much water makes mud, and the sledge sinks. Friction lives where two surfaces meet. A small change there can matter more than a big change in pulling. The story also quietly asks who gets the credit for great work.
ask: In the story, the men pulled harder when Hapu was ill. Why didn't that work?
What did just the right amount of water do to the sand? What did too much water do?
Why do you think the pullers laughed at Hapu's job of pouring water?
On her first try, Mery made mud. What did she change on her second try, and why did it work?
The painters put the tiny water-pourer at the front of their painting. Why do you think they did?

rules: Cut out the 24 cards. Shuffle them and put them in a pile, face down.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud.
Decide: in this moment, do we want more friction or less? Put the card on the GRIP mat or the SLIP mat, and say why.
Then say one way people change the friction there. For example, sand, grooves, oil, wheels or powder. A good idea wins one idea token.
If you draw a TEST IT card, everyone does the test together. The first person to explain the result wins two tokens.
When the cards run out, the player with the most tokens wins.

flow.do: 1. Lay the two mats on the floor, GRIP on one side and SLIP on the other. 2. Shuffle the 24 situation cards and put them face down in a pile. 3. Put the idea tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Friction is the grip between two things that touch. Every card shows a moment from everyday life. For each one, we decide together. Do we want more friction here, or less?
flow.kid: Put the two mats on the floor: GRIP and SLIP. Mix up the cards. Put them face down. For each card, decide. Do we want more grip, or more slip?
flow.context: This is the first step of the game Grip or Slip. It is a card game about where we want friction, and where we don't. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Find the card 'Bicycle brakes on a rainy day'. Play it together as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise with one card. 'Bicycle brakes on a rainy day.' Do we want grip or slip here?
flow.kid: Practice card: bicycle brakes on a rainy day. Grip or slip? Tap your answer.

ask.q: Why do we want grip for brakes?
good: The brakes must rub the wheel to stop it.
Rain makes things slippery, so we need extra grip.

check.q: Bicycle brakes on a rainy day. What do we want?
check.why: Brakes work by rubbing against the wheel. Friction from that rubbing slows the wheel down. Rain makes the wheel wet and slippery, so the brakes grip less. That is why we want more friction here, not less. Picking SLIP usually means thinking 'slippery is the problem' instead of 'grip is what we need'.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player draws a card, reads it out and puts it on a mat. 2. They say why. 3. They say one way people change the friction there. 4. Give one idea token for each good way.
flow.say: When you put your card down, tell me how people make that thing grip more, or slip more.
flow.kid: Take turns. Read your card. Put it on GRIP or SLIP. Then say how people change the friction there. Each good idea wins a 💡 token.
flow.parent: Good answers for more grip: grooves, rubber, sand, grit, or pressing harder. For less friction: oil, water, soap, powder, wheels or polishing. Some cards are tricky. The violin bow needs grip. Players rub a sticky resin called rosin on it. The slide and the carrom board need slip. The matchstick needs grip, because the rubbing makes the heat that lights it.

flow.do: When a TEST IT card comes up, stop and do the test together. Everyone guesses first.
flow.say: Before we test it, everyone guess what will happen. Then we'll try it and see who was right.
flow.kid: A TEST IT card! First, guess what will happen. Then do the test. Were you right?

ask.q: One TEST IT card asks you to push an empty tumbler, then a tumbler full of rice. Why was the full one harder to push?
good: It is heavier, so it presses on the table harder.

flow.think: If you pressed down on the empty tumbler with one finger, would it be harder to push? Why?

flow.do: 1. Count everyone's tokens to find the winner. 2. Then look at the two piles of cards together.
flow.say: Look at both piles. Which is bigger: the moments where we want more friction, or the moments where we want less?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Who won? Now look at the two piles. Which pile is bigger? Is friction mostly a friend, or a nuisance?
flow.think: Is friction a good force or a bad force? Or is that the wrong question?

games.title: The Day the World Lost Its Grip

printables.title: A day board with 6 moments
items: 1 Waking up and getting out of bed

printables.title: 12 twist cards
items: Friction comes back for just ONE thing. Choose it.
Your shoes keep their friction, but nothing else does.
You can switch friction on and off with a clap.
You need to stop a rolling ball.
A friend falls. How do you help?
Invent a tool that works without friction.

printables.title: Idea sheet
items: What would happen with no friction?

rules: Roll a dice. Find that number on the day board. That is your moment of the day.
Imagine that moment with no friction anywhere. Act it out or draw it.
Then take a twist card and change your story to fit it.
The other players give points. One point if your idea is true to science. One point for the most creative idea.
After 6 rounds, everyone votes. Would you switch friction back on?

flow.do: 1. Put the day board in the middle. 2. Put the twist cards face down beside it. 3. Have a dice ready.
flow.say: Imagine you wake up tomorrow and friction has disappeared from the whole world. Everything is slippery. Not just ice-slippery. Perfectly slippery.
flow.kid: Imagine you wake up tomorrow. Friction has vanished from the whole world. Everything is perfectly slippery. What happens? Let's find out.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Day the World Lost Its Grip. In this game, you imagine a whole day with no friction at all. Friction is the grip between things that touch.

flow.do: 1. Take turns rolling the dice and going to that moment on the board. 2. Imagine it with no friction, and act it out or draw it. 3. Take a twist card and change the story. 4. The others give points.
flow.say: Roll the dice. What happens at that moment with no friction? Act it out!
flow.kid: Roll the dice. Go to that moment. What happens with no friction? Act it out or draw it. Then pick a twist card.

ask.q: With no friction, could you get out of bed?
good: My hands couldn't push on or hold the bed.
Food would slide out of my hand.

ask.q: Once you started moving, could you stop?
good: No. I'd keep sliding until I hit something.

flow.parent: Science check: with no friction you could not walk at all. Your feet could not push back on the floor. Knots would come undone, and the threads in clothes would slide apart. A moving thing would never stop unless it hit something.

flow.do: Share the funniest and cleverest ideas. Then check together which ones were true to science.
flow.say: Which of our ideas were really true to science? Which were just funny?
flow.kid: Which ideas were true to science? Tap the ones you think would really happen.

check.q: With no friction at all, could you walk forward?
options: Yes, and more easily than now
No, your feet would slip back and you couldn't push off
check.why: To walk, your foot pushes backwards on the ground. Friction pushes your foot forwards in return, and that moves you. With no friction, your foot would just slide back. You would stay in the same place. Picking 'more easily' usually means thinking friction only slows us down.

flow.do: Hold a final vote. Would everyone switch friction back on?
flow.say: Final vote. Would you switch friction back on? What would you switch it on for first?
flow.kid: Last question. Would you switch friction back on? What would you switch it on for first?
flow.think: Which jobs does friction do for you that you never notice until they stop?

items.p: Friction is a force. Where does it act?
opts: Only on things that are moving fast, like cars
items.why: Friction happens wherever two surfaces touch and one is trying to slide over the other. Picking 'moving fast' usually means friction is linked only with speed. But friction also holds still things in place, like a shoe on a slope. Picking 'empty space' usually mixes friction up with gravity, which pulls without touching.
items.art: A shoe on the ground with the contact place glowing.

items.p: Which way does friction push?
opts: The same way the thing is moving
Nowhere, because friction is not a push or a pull
items.why: Friction pushes against sliding. So it slows moving things down, or stops still things from starting to slide. Picking 'the same way' often means friction is seen as a helper that carries things along. Picking 'downwards' usually mixes friction up with gravity.

items.p: A ball rolling on grass slows down and stops because of ____.
items.why: The grass rubs against the ball. That rubbing is friction, and it slows the ball down.

items.p: Sort these moments. Do we want MORE friction or LESS friction?
items: a shoe on a wet floor
a carrom striker on the board
items.why: We want more friction where we need to hold on, stop or push off. We want less where things should glide smoothly.

items.p: You give a toy car the same push on four different floors. Which floor will it roll furthest on?
items.why: Smooth tiles have the least friction. So the car slows down the least and rolls furthest. Picking carpet or grass often means soft feels smooth. But soft surfaces squash under the wheels and hold them back.
items.art: A toy car on four surfaces.

items.p: Rough surfaces usually have more friction than smooth ones.
items.why: True. The bumps on rough surfaces catch on each other more. So it is harder to slide.

items.p: Friction only causes problems.
items.why: False. We need friction to walk, hold things, write and stop. It does cause some problems too, like wearing things out.

items.p: Match each thing to what it does to friction.
items.why: Slippery things like oil and powder lower friction. Grooves and gritty sand give more grip.

items.p: Rub your hands together fast for 10 seconds. How do they feel?
opts: Colder, because air rushes past them
items.why: Friction turns the movement of your hands into heat. Picking 'colder' usually means the child is thinking of a fan, where moving air cools us. Rubbing is different: it makes heat.

items.p: Something slippery that we put between two surfaces to lower friction is called a ____.
items.why: Oil, water, soap and powder are all lubricants.

items.p: Bicycle tyres have bumpy patterns called tread. Why?
opts: To make the tyre roll faster
items.why: Tread helps the tyre grip the road. On wet roads, its grooves also let water escape. Picking 'roll faster' often means the child thinks less touching is always better. Tread is about grip, not speed.

items.p: Think of a heavy box on the floor. Which is usually harder?
opts: Keeping it moving once it slides
They are always exactly the same
items.why: It is usually harder to start something sliding than to keep it sliding. The starting grip, called static friction, is a little stronger. Picking 'keeping it moving' often comes from feeling tired after pushing for a long time. That tiredness is real, but the biggest push is needed right at the start.

items.p: A forcemeter is a tool that measures how strong a pull is. It measures in ____.
items.why: The newton is the unit of force. Its short form is N.

items.p: Why is it hard to walk on very slippery ice? Use the word friction in your answer.
items.a: There is very little friction between my shoes and the ice. When I push my foot back to step forward, it slides instead of gripping. So I can't push myself forward.
items.why: Walking needs friction. Your foot pushes back on the ground, and friction pushes you forward.

items.p: Name two places at home where you are glad there is friction. Say why for each one.
items.a: Any two good examples. For example, the bathroom mat stops me slipping when the floor is wet. My pencil grips the paper, so it leaves a line when I write.
items.why: Any two correct examples, each with a reason, are right.

items.p: Draw a shoe resting on a slope. Draw one arrow for the way the shoe would slide. Draw another arrow for friction.
items.a: The slide arrow points down the slope. The friction arrow points up the slope, along the surface.
items.why: Friction acts along the surface, against the way the shoe would slide.
items.art: A blank slope with a shoe on it.

items.p: Riya pulls a box of books across the floor with a forcemeter. The full box needs 8 newtons. The half-empty box needs 4 newtons. Look at the pictures. Why does the full box need more pull?
opts: The full box presses down harder, so there is more friction
The half-empty box is smoother underneath
The full box is bigger, so more of it touches the floor
items.why: The full box is heavier, so it presses on the floor harder. Pressing harder gives more friction. 8 newtons is twice 4 newtons. Picking 'more of it touches' is a very common idea. But it is the same box, with the same bottom on the floor. Only how hard it presses has changed.
items.context: A forcemeter is a tool with a spring inside. It shows how hard you are pulling, in units called newtons. This question compares pulling a full box and a half-empty box.

items.p: In the slope test, a shoe started to slide when the raised end of the board was 16 cm high. A sock slid when the end was only 8 cm high. Look at the chart. Which grips better?
items.why: The shoe stayed put on a much steeper slope. The steeper the slope something can stay on, the more friction it has. Picking 'the sock' usually means a lower number looked better. In this test, higher is better.
items.context: This question is about the slope test. You put a shoe on a flat board, then slowly lift one end until the shoe slides. The higher the end goes first, the better the shoe grips.

chart.title: How high the board's end went before each one slid

items.p: The shoe stayed on until the board's end was 16 cm high. The sock slid at 8 cm. The shoe's height was ____ times the sock's height.
items.why: 16 divided by 8 is 2. So the shoe's height was 2 times the sock's. You can check: 8 + 8 = 16.
items.context: This question is about the slope test. You put a shoe on a flat board, then slowly lift one end until the shoe slides. The higher the end goes first, the better the shoe grips.

chart.title: How high the board's end went before each one slid

items.p: In cricket, bowlers polish the ball by rubbing it on their trousers. They also wear shoes with spikes. Why?
opts: Polishing makes one side smooth, so the ball swings in the air. The spikes give grip on the pitch.
Both are to make more friction
Both are to make less friction
Polishing makes the ball sticky, so it grips the bat
items.why: Polishing makes one side of the ball smoother. This changes how air flows round it, so it swings. Spikes dig into the ground and give the bowler more grip. Picking 'both more' or 'both less' usually means the child expects one rule for everything. In cricket, people want less friction in one place and more in another.

items.p: Sort these ways people change friction.
items: sprinkling sand on a slippery path
items.why: Wheels, oil and wax help things move easily. Sand, rubber and chalk help things grip.

items.p: Why do old temple steps have a dip worn in the middle?
opts: The builders made them that way
Millions of feet rubbed tiny bits away over hundreds of years
Rain fell only in the middle
Heavy people pressed the stone down, like clay
items.why: Friction slowly rubs surfaces away, even hard stone. This is called wear. Picking 'pressed down like clay' usually means stone is pictured as soft. Hard stone does not squash. It slowly wears away.

items.p: In empty space, a ball you push would keep going for ever, because there is nothing to rub against.
items.why: True. With no ground or air to rub on, nothing slows it down. It keeps going until it hits something, or gravity pulls it off course.

items.p: Which way would move a heavy stone most easily?
items.why: Rolling has much less friction than sliding. Picking 'more people' often means the child thinks the answer is always more pulling. Changing the surface, or rolling instead of sliding, can matter more.
items.context: Before machines, people moved huge stones for temples and statues by hand. This question asks which way is easiest.

items.p: Match each person to their idea about friction.
pairs: Leonardo da Vinci, an Italian artist and inventor
wrote rules of friction in his notebooks, around 1493
published the rules of friction, in 1699
saw that things stop because of friction, not because stopping is natural
items.why: Leonardo found the rules first, but did not publish them. So Amontons usually gets the credit.
items.context: This question is about three people from the history of friction science.

items.p: Why might the man in the Egyptian painting be pouring water on the sand?
opts: To cool the hot sand for the men's feet
Damp sand lets the sledge slide with less friction
To wash the dust off the statue
items.why: The right amount of water makes sand firm. Then the sledge slides on top, instead of digging in and pushing up a hill of sand. Picking 'to cool the sand' is a sensible guess about the hot desert. But the water is poured right in front of the sledge, where it meets the sand.
items.context: About 3,900 years ago, Egyptians painted workers dragging a giant statue across the sand on a wooden sledge. One man at the front pours water on the sand.

items.p: What happens if you pour too MUCH water on the sand?
opts: It gets even easier, because more water means more slippery
The sand becomes mud and the sledge sinks in
The water dries up too fast to matter
items.why: A little water makes sand firm. Too much water turns it into soft mud, and the heavy sledge sinks in. Picking 'even easier' is a very common idea: if a little helps, more must help more. Here, it does not.
items.context: This question is about dragging a heavy sledge across sand, as the ancient Egyptians did. A little water on the sand helps the sledge slide.

items.p: A heavy almirah, a tall steel cupboard, will not move. Give two different ways to make it easier to push. Explain each one using the word friction.
items.a: One way: take things out of it. Then it presses down on the floor less, so there is less friction. Another way: put rollers or a folded cloth under it. Then it rolls, or slides, with less friction.
items.why: Pressing down less, adding a slippery layer, or rolling instead of sliding all lower friction.

items.p: Why do your hands get warm when you rub them together? Where does the movement go?
items.a: Friction between my hands turns some of the movement into heat. The movement does not vanish. It becomes warmth.
items.why: Friction changes movement energy into heat energy.

items.p: A box is being pushed to the right across the floor. Show all the forces on it, with one arrow for each.
items.obj: a box pushed to the right
items.why: Friction acts against the push, so it points left. Gravity pulls the box down. The floor pushes it up.

items.p: Design a shoe sole for walking on the wet, mossy steps of a ghat. Label two features that give more grip.
items.a: Good features include soft rubber, deep grooves to let water out, small bumps or studs, and a wide flat area that touches the stone.
items.why: Soft rubber and grooves give more grip on wet surfaces.
items.context: A ghat is a row of wide stone steps going down to a river. When they are wet and mossy, people slip.

items.p: A brick is pulled lying flat, on its big side. Then it is pulled standing on its thin edge. Look at the pictures. The forcemeter shows about the same pull both times. What does this tell us?
opts: Friction depends a lot on how much area touches
For a hard brick, friction hardly depends on how much area touches
The thin edge should cut in and grip more
items.why: For hard things, the touching area hardly matters. What matters is the materials, and how hard they press together. Guillaume Amontons wrote this down in 1699, and it surprised people. Picking 'depends a lot on area' means going with what feels true, not with what the forcemeter shows. Many grown-ups believed that for hundreds of years.
items.context: A forcemeter is a tool with a spring inside. It shows how hard you are pulling, in units called newtons. This question is about pulling a brick two ways.

show.caption: Brick on its thin edge: 6 newtons

items.p: If area hardly matters for a brick, why do racing cars have very wide tyres?
opts: The rule only works for hard things. Soft, sticky rubber grips more with more area.
The rule is wrong for everything
items.why: The 'area hardly matters' rule breaks down for soft, sticky things like tyre rubber. Picking 'wrong for everything' misses that the rule still works well for hard things like bricks and wooden blocks.
items.context: For a hard brick, the area touching the ground hardly changes the friction. This question is about tyres, which are soft.

items.p: Scientists completely understand why ice is slippery.
items.why: False. Scientists still argue about it. Ideas include a slippery, almost wet layer on top, melting caused by sliding, and loose molecules that roll.

items.p: What could change Aristotle's mind?
opts: Seeing a ball roll further and further on smoother surfaces, as if with no friction it would never stop
Seeing a ball stop on grass
Seeing a heavy ball stop sooner than a light one
items.why: Galileo saw that less friction means a longer roll. So friction stops things, not nature. Picking 'a ball stopping on grass' shows just what Aristotle already saw. It fits his idea, so it would not change his mind.
items.context: Aristotle was a thinker in ancient Greece, about 2,350 years ago. He thought moving things stop because stopping is natural.

items.p: Which of these is NOT caused by friction?
opts: A cycle stopping when you brake
A magnet pulling a pin from across the table
items.why: The magnet pulls the pin without touching it. Friction only happens where surfaces touch. Picking the match or the shoe usually means heat and wear are not yet linked to rubbing. Both come from friction.

items.p: Engineers estimate that nearly a ____ of all the energy people use is lost to friction and wear in machines.
items.why: In 2017, two engineers, Holmberg and Erdemir, estimated about 23 out of every 100 units. That is nearly a quarter, which is 25 out of 100.
items.context: This question is about how much of the world's energy is wasted by friction in machines.

answer_chart.title: Of all the energy people use, how much is lost to friction and wear (an estimate)
answer_chart.unit: out of every 100 units of energy

data.label: Lost to friction and wear: 23 out of 100

items.p: Put these in order, from MOST friction to LEAST: ice, rubber mat, polished floor, sandpaper.
items.why: Rough sandpaper grips most. A rubber mat grips well. A polished floor is slippery. Ice is the most slippery of all.

items.p: Two notebooks have their pages laid over each other like this. They are very hard to pull apart. Why?
opts: The pages are glued together a little
Hundreds of pages each add a little friction, and pulling squeezes them together even more
The books are too heavy to lift
items.why: Each page grips only a tiny bit. But hundreds of tiny grips add up. Pulling also squeezes the pages tighter, which adds more friction. Picking glue or magnets usually means the child expects a hidden force. The surprise is that ordinary friction, added up many times, is enough.
items.context: In the Books That Won't Let Go experiment, you lay the pages of two notebooks over each other. You take one page from each book in turn, like shuffling cards.

items.p: Why might Leonardo's friction rules have been forgotten for 200 years?
opts: His notebooks were not published, so other scientists never read them
Amontons copied him and kept it secret
Nobody cared about friction back then
items.why: In science, the credit usually goes to whoever publishes. Work that is never published can be lost. Picking 'copied him' is a common guess when credit goes to the wrong person. There is no evidence for that. Amontons worked it out for himself.
items.context: Leonardo da Vinci, the Italian artist and inventor, wrote down the rules of friction around 1493. But most books credit Guillaume Amontons, who published them in 1699.

items.p: In the story, the men pulled harder, but the sledge would not move. Then Mery poured just enough water on the sand. Why did changing the sand work better than pulling harder? Use the word friction.
items.a: Dry sand piled up in front of the sledge and held it back. Damp sand stayed firm, so the sledge slid on top with less friction. Pulling harder only pushed the sledge deeper into the dry sand.
items.why: Friction depends on both surfaces that touch. Changing the sand changed the friction, so a smaller pull was enough.
items.context: In this unit's story, a giant statue is dragged on a sledge in ancient Egypt. Hapu's only job was to pour water on the sand in front of it. The men laughed, but without the water the statue would not move.

items.p: Invent one machine that would work better WITHOUT friction, and one that could not work without it. Explain both.
items.a: For example: a wheel that turned with no friction would waste no energy, so a cycle would roll further. But brakes could not work without friction, because they must rub the wheel to stop it.
items.why: A good answer shows that friction is useful in some places and wasteful in others.

items.p: How could you design a test to find out which idea matters more?
items.a: For example: take two pieces of the same material. Make one very rough, and polish the other very smooth. Pull each with a forcemeter. If the rough piece grips more, bumps matter more. If the very polished piece grips more, sticking atoms matter more.
items.why: A good test changes only one thing, here the roughness, and keeps everything else the same.
items.context: Scientists have had two ideas about why surfaces grip. One idea is that tiny bumps catch on each other, like the teeth of two combs. The other is that the atoms of the two surfaces stick together.

items.p: Astronauts inside a space station float. They hold on to handles to stay in place. Why can't they just stand on the floor?
opts: They float instead of pressing down on the floor, so their feet get almost no friction
There is no air in the space station
items.why: Friction depends on how hard two surfaces press together. Floating astronauts hardly press on the floor at all, so their feet get almost no grip. Picking 'no air' is a common mix-up. The space station is full of air, so astronauts can breathe.

items.p: Is friction a 'good' force or a 'bad' force? Give your opinion, with one reason for each side.
items.a: A balanced answer. For example: friction is good because it lets us walk and stop. It is bad because it wastes energy and wears things out. So perhaps it depends on where it is.
items.why: There is no single right answer. What counts is giving a reason for each side.

items.p: Draw a close-up of two 'smooth' surfaces touching, as a very strong microscope would show them. Mark the places where they really touch.
items.a: Two bumpy edges, like mountain ranges, touching only at a few peaks. The touching peaks are marked.
items.why: Even smooth surfaces are bumpy close up. They touch only at a few tiny points.

items.p: Deep down, where does friction come from?
opts: Atoms tugging on each other with electric force
items.why: Friction comes from electric pushes and pulls between the atoms of the two surfaces. Picking 'tiny hooks' is close to the old bumps idea, and bumps do play a part. But deep down, even bumps grip through electric forces. Picking gravity mixes up two different forces.

items.p: Superfluid helium, once stirred, keeps swirling without slowing down. Why?
opts: It has no friction at all
It is very heavy, so it keeps going
It is very cold, and cold things move faster
items.why: With no friction, nothing turns its movement into heat. So it does not slow down. Picking 'very heavy' usually means heavy things are thought to keep going longer. What really stops moving things is friction.
items.context: A superfluid is a liquid with no friction at all. Scientists make it by cooling helium to about 271 degrees below zero.

items.p: Friction from the ocean tides is very slowly making Earth's days longer.
items.why: True. The tides rub on the sea floor, and this slowly brakes the Earth's spin. About 400 million years ago, a day lasted only about 22 hours.
items.context: Tides are the sea rising and falling, about twice a day, mostly because the Moon's gravity pulls on the water.

answer_chart.title: How long one day lasted, then and now

items.p: A film shows a box sliding across a floor and stopping. How could you tell if the film was playing backwards?
items.a: Played backwards, the box would start moving all by itself, pushed by a warm floor. That never happens. Friction turns movement into heat, but it never turns heat back into movement like that.
items.why: Friction only works one way. Some scientists link this to the 'arrow of time', the fact that time only goes forwards.
items.context: Friction turns movement into heat. But heat never turns back into the same movement by itself.

experiments.title: The Slope Test: which sole grips best?
experiments.question: Which of our shoes and socks grips best?
experiments.predict: Before you test anything, line up the shoes and socks. Put the one you think grips best first, and the one you think grips least last. Then say why you put them in that order.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, keep everything the same except the shoe. Use the same board, and lift it at the same slow speed every time. Test each shoe 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a long flat board, about 30 to 40 cm long, such as a chopping board or a tray (a big hardback book also works)
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Use light shoes, like chappals or slippers. Keep your fingers out of the way when the shoe slides off.

schedule.what: Guess which shoe grips best. Test each shoe 3 times on the slope. Write down the heights. Then draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart. Draw one bar for each shoe. Make each bar as tall as that shoe's middle height.

flow.do: 1. Collect 3 or 4 different shoes or socks. Try to include a rubber chappal and a sock. 2. Ask your child to put them in a line, best grip first.
flow.say: Which of these do you think will grip best? Put them in a line. Put the best gripper first and the most slippery last.
flow.kid: Find 3 or 4 different shoes or socks. Put them in a line. Which do you think grips best? Put that one first.

ask.q: Why did you put that one first?

flow.context: This is the first step of the slope test. You find out which shoe grips best by lifting a board until the shoe slides.

flow.do: 1. Lay the board flat on the floor. 2. Put the first shoe on the board, sole down, near one end. 3. That is the end you will lift.
flow.say: We'll lift this end slowly until the shoe slides. The higher we can lift it before the shoe slides, the better the shoe grips.
flow.kid: Lay the board flat. Put a shoe near one end, sole down. You will lift that end slowly. Higher before sliding means better grip.

flow.do: 1. Lift the shoe's end slowly, about one finger-width each second. 2. Stop the moment the shoe starts to slide. 3. Hold the board still. Measure from the floor to the top of the lifted end. 4. Write the number in the table. 5. Do this 3 times for each shoe.
flow.say: Lift slowly and steadily. Stop the moment it slides. Now let's measure how high the end is, from the floor up.
flow.kid: Lift slowly. When the shoe slides, stop! Measure how high the end is. Write it in the table. Test each shoe 3 times.
flow.parent: Keep the lifting speed the same each time, so the test is fair. If one try is very different, that's fine. That's why we do three. To find the middle value, put the three numbers in order and take the middle one. The heights depend on how long your board is, so use the same board for every test. If a sock crumples, fold it into a flat pad.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the middle values, with one bar for each shoe.
flow.say: Let's turn the numbers into a picture. Each shoe gets one bar. The taller the bar, the higher the board went before that shoe slid.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each shoe. Make it as tall as its middle number. A taller bar means better grip.

check.q: In the slope test bar chart, a taller bar means the shoe…
check.why: The bar shows how high the board's end was when the shoe started to slide. A shoe that grips well stays put on a steeper board, so its bar is taller. Picking 'grips less' usually means thinking 'higher number means more slipping'.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how high the board's end went before each one slid
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: 1. Compare the results with the line of guesses you made at the start. 2. If you have time, wipe the board with a damp cloth and test the best gripper once more. See if the height changes.
flow.say: Were your guesses right? Look at the shoes that gripped best. What do they have in common?
flow.kid: Were your guesses right? Look at the best gripper. What is it made of? What pattern is on its bottom?
flow.think: If you had to climb wet rocks at a waterfall, which shoe would you wear? Why?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say or write three things. What do I think? What did I see? Why did it happen?
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the rubber chappal grips best. What I saw: it stayed on until the board was 16 cm high, but the sock slid at 8 cm. Why: rubber is soft, so it presses into the tiny bumps of the board and grips them.

experiments.context: This is the slope test. You put a shoe on a flat board, then slowly lift one end until the shoe slides. The higher you can lift it first, the better that shoe grips.

experiments.title: The Books That Won't Let Go
experiments.question: Can the friction between paper pages be stronger than you?
experiments.predict: Guess first. If you lay the pages of two notebooks over each other, will they be easy or hard to pull apart? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Try with 10 pages laid together, then 30 pages, then all the pages. Pull the same way each time, holding each book by its spine. Change only the number of pages.
results_table: How many pages were laid together
Easy, hard or impossible to pull apart?

materials.item: two thick notebooks of the same size, each with about 150 pages or more, such as school long books or old paperback books

experiments.safety: Pull gently, so you don't tear the books.

schedule.what: Lay the pages together and try to pull the books apart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write one sentence about why it got harder.

flow.do: 1. Put the two notebooks on a table, with their spines facing outwards. Slide them together so their pages overlap by about half a page. 2. Flick down one page from the first book. 3. Flick down one page from the second book on top of it. 4. Keep going, one page from each book in turn, like shuffling cards.
flow.say: We'll lay the pages of these two books in between each other. One page from this book, then one page from that book.
flow.kid: Put the two notebooks open edge to open edge. Lay down a page from one book. Then a page from the other on top. Keep going, like shuffling cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Books That Won't Let Go experiment. Here you lay the pages of two notebooks over each other.

flow.do: 1. Lay 10 pages together, then try to pull the books apart by their spines. 2. Separate them. Lay 30 pages together and pull again. 3. Last, lay all the pages together and pull.
flow.say: Try to pull them apart. Now let's try with more pages. What changes?
flow.kid: Lay 10 pages together. Pull the books apart. Easy? Now try 30 pages. Now try all of them. Can you still do it?

ask.q: Why is it harder with more pages?
good: Each page adds a little friction.
More surfaces are touching each other.

flow.parent: Laying all the pages takes a few minutes. That is normal. If the books still pull apart easily, make the pages overlap more.

flow.do: Talk together about why it got so hard.
flow.say: Each page grips only a tiny bit. But hundreds of tiny grips add up. And when you pull, the pages squeeze together tighter. On a TV science show, two big phone books woven together like this could not be pulled apart even by two cars.
flow.kid: Each page grips only a tiny bit. But hundreds of tiny grips add up! Pulling squeezes the pages tighter, too. Even two cars could not pull two big books apart!
flow.think: Can lots of small things together be stronger than one big thing? Where else do you see that?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say or write three things. What do I think? What did I see? Why did it happen?
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: lots of pages laid together are almost impossible to pull apart. What I saw: with 10 pages they pulled apart easily, but with all the pages I couldn't do it. Why: every page adds a little friction, and pulling squeezes them tighter.

experiments.context: In this experiment you weave the pages of two notebooks together, one page from each in turn. Then you try to pull them apart. It shows how many tiny frictions add up.
