experiments.title: Pour the Water Like Hapu
experiments.question: Does wet sand make a sledge easier to pull? How much water is best?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will dry sand, damp sand or soaked sand be easiest to pull a loaded box across? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Keep everything the same except the sand. Use the same box, with the same load inside, and pull it the same distance. Measure the pull with a forcemeter. If you have no forcemeter, tie a rubber band to the string and measure how far it stretches with a ruler.
results_table: Pull needed (newtons), or rubber band stretch (cm)
What the sand did in front of the box

materials.item: a baking tray or a shallow box, filled with dry sand about two fingers deep. Take a few handfuls from a building site or a sand pit, or buy a small bag of play sand or aquarium sand.
a small flat-bottomed plastic lunch box or tin to be the 'sledge', with a half-kilo packet of dal, rice or salt inside to make it heavy. A cardboard box goes soggy on wet sand.
a piece of string, about as long as your arm
a forcemeter, or a rubber band and a ruler
a cup of water and a spoon

experiments.safety: Do this on newspaper, on the floor or on a balcony. A grown-up helps with the sand and water.

schedule.what: Pull the box across dry sand, then damp sand, then soaked sand.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw what the sand did in front of the box each time.

flow.do: 1. Spread dry sand evenly in the tray, about two fingers deep. 2. Put the packet of dal, rice or salt in the box, and close the lid. 3. Tie the string to the box. 4. Tie the forcemeter's hook, or a rubber band, to the other end of the string.
flow.say: This box is our stone statue on its sledge. Let's see how hard it is to pull across dry desert sand.
flow.kid: Spread dry sand in the tray. Put the dal packet in the box. Tie the string to the box. Tie the forcemeter to the string. This box is your stone statue!
flow.context: This is the first step of the wet sand experiment. You build a tiny model of an Egyptian statue being dragged across the desert on a sledge.

flow.do: 1. Pull the string slowly and steadily, so the box moves across the dry sand. 2. Read the forcemeter while the box is moving, or measure how far the rubber band has stretched. 3. Watch the sand at the front of the box.
flow.say: Pull slowly. Look at the front of the box. What is the sand doing?
flow.kid: Pull slowly. Read the number on the forcemeter. Look at the front of the box. Is sand piling up?

ask.q: What did the sand do in front of the box?

flow.do: 1. Sprinkle water on the sand, one spoon at a time. Mix it in well after each spoon, so all the sand gets damp. 2. Stop when all the sand has just turned darker, but is not wet or muddy. Smooth the top. 3. Pull the box again and read the forcemeter.
flow.say: Now we'll pour like Hapu, the water-pourer in our story. Just enough to darken the sand, but not enough to make mud.
flow.kid: Now be Hapu, the water-pourer! Sprinkle one spoon of water at a time. Stop when the sand turns darker. Not muddy! Pull again. Is it easier?
flow.parent: If you see little difference between dry and damp sand, put a heavier load in the box and pull more slowly. Damp sand should feel firm, like sand for building a sandcastle.

flow.do: 1. Pour in lots more water, until the sand is soaked and muddy. 2. Pull the box again and read the forcemeter.
flow.say: Now let's do what Mery, Hapu's daughter in the story, did on her first try. She poured far too much water.
flow.kid: Now pour lots of water, like Mery in the story. She poured too much at first! Pull again. What happens?

check.q: Which sand was easiest to pull the box across?
check.why: Damp sand sticks together into a firm path, so the box rides on top. Dry sand is loose and piles up in front of the box. Soaked sand turns to mud and the box sinks in. Just-damp sand needs the smallest pull. Picking soaked sand usually means thinking 'more water is always more slippery'.

flow.do: Put the three results side by side and compare them.
flow.say: In 2014, scientists in Amsterdam did this same test. They found the right amount of water could roughly halve the pull. Why do you think the damp sand worked best?
flow.kid: In 2014, scientists did this test too. The right amount of water made the pull about half! Why did damp sand work best?
flow.think: The workers in Egypt knew this about 3,900 years before scientists explained it. How do you think they found out?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say or write three things. What do I think? What did I see? Why did it happen?
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: just-damp sand is easiest for the sledge. What I saw: dry sand needed 6 newtons and piled up in front of the box. Damp sand needed only 3 newtons. Soaked sand turned to mud. Why: a little water holds the sand grains together, so the box slides on top instead of digging in.

activities.title: Friction Hunt

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil, to list what you find

activities.safety: Go outdoors only with a grown-up.

schedule.what: Hunt for friction indoors, then on a short walk.

activities.record: Find 12 places. Write each one down, and write GRIP or SLIP next to it.

flow.do: Explain the hunt to your child, and give them the paper and pencil.
flow.say: We're friction detectives. Let's find 12 places where friction is helping. Or places where people have tried to make it smaller.
flow.kid: You are a friction detective! Find 12 places where friction helps. Or places where people made it smaller.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Friction Hunt. Friction is the grip between two things that touch.

flow.do: Hunt around the home, then outside. Look at shoe soles, tyres, mats and door hinges. Look at the gas knob, a jar lid, stairs, a bicycle chain and a slide.
flow.say: For each one, is it built for grip or for slip? How can you tell?
flow.kid: For each place, decide. Is it made for GRIP or for SLIP? Look for grooves, rubber, oil, wheels and powder.
flow.parent: Good finds: the grooved bottom of a chappal, the rubber feet under a mixer, and rough tiles near the bathroom. Also grease on a cycle chain, old worn steps, and a doorknob polished smooth by hands.

flow.do: Ask each person to share their best find.
flow.say: Which find surprised you most?
flow.kid: Which find surprised you most? Take a photo or draw it.
flow.think: Did someone design these things on purpose? Who might it have been?

activities.context: This is a hunt around your home and street. You look for places where friction helps, or where people made it smaller on purpose.

activities.title: Hot Hands: feel friction make heat

materials.item: an eraser and a sheet of paper

schedule.what: Feel the heat that friction makes.

activities.record: Write down how your hands felt after 10 rubs, 20 rubs and 30 rubs. Were they cool, a bit warm or hot?

flow.do: 1. Rub your palms together fast, 10 times. 2. Touch your cheek with your palms. 3. Do it again with 20 rubs, then with 30 rubs.
flow.say: Rub your palms together 10 times, fast. Now touch your cheek. How does it feel? Let's try 20 rubs. Now 30.
flow.kid: Rub your hands together fast, 10 times. Touch your cheek. Now try 20 rubs. Now 30. What do you feel?
flow.context: This is the first step of Hot Hands. You rub your palms together and feel friction turn movement into warmth.

flow.do: 1. Rub an eraser hard on a sheet of paper for 20 seconds. 2. Straight away, touch the rubbed part of the paper and the end of the eraser.
flow.say: Feel the paper and the eraser. Are they warm? Where do you think the warmth came from?
flow.kid: Rub an eraser hard on paper for 20 seconds. Touch the paper and the eraser. Are they warm? Why?

check.q: Why does rubbing make things warm?
options: The eraser keeps heat inside it
check.why: When two things rub, their atoms tug and snap free again and again. Each snap leaves the atoms jiggling a little faster. Jiggling atoms are what heat is. So rubbing turns movement into warmth.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up strikes a match while the child watches from a safe distance. 2. Talk about how people made fire by rubbing sticks, long before matches.
flow.say: A match uses friction. Rubbing it on the box makes its tip hot enough to catch fire. Long before matches, people made fire by rubbing sticks together.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to strike a match. Watch from a safe distance. Rubbing makes it hot enough to burn! Long ago, people made fire by rubbing sticks.
flow.think: Making fire by rubbing sticks needs fast, hard rubbing for a long time. Why would a slow, gentle rub not work?

activities.context: This activity lets you feel friction making heat, using only your hands, an eraser and some paper.

activities.title: Act It Out: The Frictionless Kitchen

materials.item: some open space to move around in

activities.safety: Act on a soft floor, like a mat or carpet. Pretend to slide. Don't really slide.

schedule.what: Act out a dinner with no friction.

activities.record: Draw your favourite moment from the play.

flow.do: Help each player choose a role. They can be the cook or the hungry eater. Or the roti that rolls away, or the laddoo that won't stop sliding.
flow.say: We're going to act out making dinner in a kitchen where friction has disappeared. Everything is perfectly slippery.
flow.kid: Pick your role. You can be the cook or the hungry eater. Or the roti that rolls away. Or the laddoo that won't stop sliding!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Frictionless Kitchen play. Friction is the grip between things that touch. In this play, it has disappeared.

flow.do: Act out cooking and eating with no friction. Remember the rules: nothing can be held, nothing stops once it moves, and nobody can walk.
flow.say: Remember: you can't walk. Things slide out of your hands. And nothing stops once it starts moving!
flow.kid: Act it out! You can't walk. Nothing stays in your hand. Nothing stops once it starts moving.

flow.do: Talk about which parts of the play were true to science.
flow.say: Which parts of our play would really happen if there were no friction?
flow.kid: Which parts of your play would really happen?
flow.think: Friction is invisible, but everything depends on it. What else is invisible, but everywhere?
flow.parent: With no friction you truly could not walk, because your feet would slip instead of pushing off. Food would slide out of your hands. A rolling roti would never stop until it hit something.

activities.title: Slide the Tumbler, Slide the Sock

materials.item: a steel tumbler, three things to lay on a table (a cotton cloth, a towel and a plastic bag or sheet), socks, and a smooth tiled or polished floor

activities.safety: Slide gently. First clear the floor of anything sharp or breakable.

schedule.what: Test cloths, slide in socks, and look at old soles.

activities.record: Put the cloths in order, from most grip to least. Write where you could slide in socks. Draw the bottom of an old, worn shoe.

flow.do: 1. Lay the cloth, the towel and the plastic flat on a table, side by side. 2. Put the empty tumbler at one end of the first one. 3. Give it a small tap near its bottom with one finger, so it slides without tipping over. See how far it slides. 4. Do the same on each one, with the same small tap.
flow.say: Which one do you think will stop the tumbler fastest? Why? The one that stops it fastest has the most friction.
flow.kid: Put the tumbler on a cloth. Give it a small tap with one finger. How far does it go? Try the same tap on each one.

ask.q: Which cloth would you put under a glass on a moving train's table?
good: The one with the most friction.

flow.context: This is the first step of the tumbler and sock activity. You find out which cloth has the most friction.

flow.do: 1. Let your child slide in socks on the smooth floor. 2. Then let them try to slide on a carpet or mat.
flow.say: Where do you think you will slide further, on the smooth floor or on the mat? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Slide in your socks on the smooth floor. Now try on a mat. Where can you slide? Where do you stop?
flow.think: Scientists have made a very cold liquid called a superfluid, with no friction at all. Stir it, and it keeps swirling. What would happen to you on a floor with no friction?
flow.parent: Socks slide well on smooth tiles, because there is little friction between cloth and tile. A mat grips the socks much more, so you stop.

flow.do: Look at the bottoms of an old pair of shoes together. Find where they are worn most.
flow.say: The most worn places show where your shoe rubs the ground hardest. Where are they on this shoe?
flow.kid: Turn over an old shoe. Where is it worn smooth? Friction rubbed most there. Do you walk more on your heels or your toes?

check.q: Why does the bottom of a shoe wear smooth?
options: Friction rubs tiny bits off it
check.why: Every step rubs the sole against the ground. Friction tears off tiny bits of rubber each time, too small to see. After thousands of steps, those tiny bits add up, and the sole wears smooth.

activities.title: Fridge Magnets: a model of atoms gripping

materials.item: two thin, bendy fridge magnets, the flat kind used for adverts

activities.safety: Keep magnets away from phones and bank cards.

schedule.what: Slide two magnets face to face.

activities.record: Draw what the sliding felt like. Was it smooth, bumpy or clicky?

flow.do: 1. Put the two magnets face to face, with their dark magnetic backs touching. 2. Slide one over the other. 3. Turn one magnet a quarter turn, and slide again.
flow.say: Slide one magnet over the other. What does it feel like? Why do you think it feels like that?
flow.kid: Put the dark backs of two fridge magnets together. Slide one over the other. Feel the clicks? Now turn one a quarter turn. Is it different?

ask.q: What does the sliding feel like?

flow.context: This is the first step of the fridge magnet activity. You slide two flat magnets over each other and feel them grab.
flow.parent: These magnets are made in thin stripes of north and south poles. As you slide, the stripes attract, then repel, then attract again. That is the clicky feel. Turned a quarter turn, the stripes cross, and the slide feels smoother.

flow.do: Explain how the magnets are like real friction.
flow.say: Real friction is a bit like this, but far, far tinier. Atoms of the two surfaces tug on each other with electric force. They hold for a moment, then snap free as you slide. Each snap leaves the atoms jiggling. Jiggling atoms are heat. That's why friction makes things warm.
flow.kid: Real friction is like this, but much tinier. Atoms of two surfaces tug on each other. They hold on, then snap free. Each snap makes atoms jiggle. Jiggling atoms are heat!

options: Atoms tugging on each other with electric force
check.why: Zoom right in and every surface is made of atoms. The atoms of two touching surfaces pull and push on each other with electric force. That is the grip we call friction. Surfaces do have tiny bumps, but where the bumps touch, it is atoms tugging on atoms that makes the grip.

flow.think: The force that holds you up off the floor and the force that grips your shoe are the same kind. What else might be secretly electric?

activities.context: This activity uses two thin fridge magnets. Sliding them over each other gives you a hand-sized model of how atoms grab and let go when surfaces slide.

activities.title: The Moon's Slow Goodbye (act it out)
activities.safety: Spin slowly. Stop if you feel dizzy.

schedule.what: Act out how the tides slow the Earth.

activities.record: Draw the Earth, the bulge of ocean water, and the Moon moving away.

flow.do: 1. The child stands in the middle. They are the Earth, and they turn slowly on the spot. 2. The grown-up is the Moon, and walks slowly in a big circle around the child. 3. The grown-up loops the dupatta loosely around the child's waist and holds one end. The dupatta is the ocean, pulled towards the Moon.
flow.say: You're the Earth, spinning. I'm the Moon. My gravity pulls the ocean towards me. Can you feel the ocean rubbing as you turn?
flow.kid: You are the Earth! Turn slowly. A grown-up is the Moon. The dupatta around you is the ocean. Can you feel it rub as you turn?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Moon's Slow Goodbye. Tides are the sea rising and falling, mostly because the Moon's gravity pulls on the water.

flow.do: 1. As the child turns, the rubbing dupatta slows them a little. 2. Each time the Moon goes round, the grown-up takes one small step further out.
flow.say: The ocean rubbing on the sea floor is friction. It slows the Earth's spin a tiny bit. And the Moon gets a tiny bit further away, about 3.8 centimetres every year.
flow.kid: The rubbing slows you down a tiny bit. Each time round, the Moon steps further away. The real Moon moves away as fast as fingernails grow!

check.q: About 400 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs, how long was one day?
options: Exactly 24 hours, the same as now
check.why: Tides rubbing the sea floor are slowly slowing the Earth's spin, so days were shorter long ago. Very old corals grew one thin line each day. 400 million years ago they grew about 400 lines a year. 400 days in a year means each day was only about 22 hours.

flow.do: Talk about how scientists know this. Mention the lines on ancient corals and the lasers bounced off the Moon.
flow.say: How do we know? Ancient corals grew one thin line every day. Scientists counted about 400 lines in each year of growth. So a year then had about 400 shorter days. Scientists also bounce laser light off mirrors that astronauts left on the Moon. That tells them exactly how far away it is.
flow.kid: How do we know? Very old corals grew a line every day. They grew about 400 lines a year! Scientists also bounce lasers off mirrors on the Moon.
flow.think: Even the length of a day is slowly changing. What else that seems fixed might be changing too slowly to notice?

projects.title: Grip Socks Workshop

materials.item: fabric puff paint, or a hot glue gun used only by a grown-up. No paint or glue? Sew on thin strips cut from an old balloon or rubber glove, with a grown-up's help.
the board and ruler from the slope test

projects.safety: Only a grown-up uses the hot glue gun. Let the paint dry completely before anyone wears the socks.

schedule.what: Test plain socks on the slope. Design a grip pattern. Paint the dots.
Check whether the paint is dry. If it is still soft, leave it another day.
Test the grip socks. Compare them with plain socks. Improve the design. Give them to someone who needs them.

projects.record: Write the slide height for the plain sock and for the grip sock. Draw your design. Write what you changed.

flow.do: 1. Put a plain sock flat on the board, near one end. 2. Slowly lift that end until the sock slides. 3. Measure the height of the lifted end with a ruler, and write it down.
flow.say: Socks are slippery on tiles. Let's measure exactly how slippery.
flow.kid: Put a plain sock on the board. Lift one end slowly until it slides. Measure how high the end is. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Grip Socks Workshop. First, you measure how slippery a plain sock is, using a board lifted at one end.

flow.do: Help your child draw a grip pattern on paper. Dots, lines or zigzags all work.
flow.say: Engineers design before they build. Which pattern might grip best: dots, lines or zigzags? Which parts of the sole touch the floor most?
flow.kid: Design first, like an engineer. Draw a pattern for the bottom of the sock. Dots, lines or zigzags? Put it where the sock touches the floor.

flow.do: 1. Cut a foot shape from cardboard and slide it inside the sock. It stops the paint soaking through. Lay the sock on newspaper, sole up. 2. Paint the pattern onto the sole with puff paint. 3. If you use a glue gun, a grown-up does this part.
flow.say: Let's make your design real.
flow.kid: Paint your pattern on the bottom of the socks. Using a glue gun? Ask a grown-up to do it.

flow.do: Leave the socks flat in a safe place to dry for at least a day.
flow.say: Now we wait. Good engineering needs patience.
flow.kid: Now let them dry for a whole day. Good engineers are patient!
flow.wait: Leave the socks to dry for 1 to 2 days.

flow.do: 1. Test a grip sock on the board, the same way as the plain sock. 2. Compare the two heights. 3. Talk about how to improve the design.
flow.say: How much higher does the board go now before the sock slides? What would you change?
flow.kid: Test your grip sock on the board. How high can you lift it now? What would make it even better?

check.q: A grip sock stays on the board until the end is 16 cm high. A plain sock slides at 8 cm. What does this show?
options: The grip sock held on until the board was twice as high
The grip sock and the plain sock grip the same
The grip sock grips less, because the number is bigger
check.why: The grip sock stayed on until 16 cm. The plain sock slid at 8 cm. 16 divided by 8 is 2. So the grip sock held on until the board was twice as high. A bigger number here means better grip, not worse.

flow.say: Who in our family could use these? Let's give them, and explain why they help.
flow.kid: Who could use grip socks, so they don't slip? Give them away. Explain the science!
flow.think: When you design for someone else, what do they need that you don't?

challenges.title: Move the Mountain
challenges.problem: A shoebox with 2 or 3 books inside is your 'mountain'. Your job is to move it 2 metres across the floor, using as little pull as you can.
constraints: Keep the same books inside the box for every try.
You can only use things you find at home.
Measure your pull each time with a forcemeter or a rubber band.
materials: a shoebox or small cardboard box with 2 or 3 books inside
a forcemeter, or a rubber band and a ruler
things from home, like rolling pins, round pencils, marbles, a cloth and a tray
general: Put round things under the box, like round pencils or a rolling pin. Then it rolls instead of sliding.
On a tiled floor, put a smooth cloth or tray under the box, so it slides more easily.
Pull low and steady. Remember, starting is the hardest part.
creative: Put the box on a tray, and the tray on a few marbles. The marbles roll like the ball bearings in a cycle wheel. As they roll out at the back, move them to the front.
Builders long ago moved huge stones with sledges, wooden rollers, ramps and water. Could one of these ideas help you?
Ancient Egyptians poured water on sand to help their sledges slide. Could a damp cloth under the box help? Wipe the floor dry afterwards, so nobody slips.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Draw it, try it, and measure the pull. Is it better than the others?

flow.do: 1. Hook the forcemeter or rubber band to the box, using string if needed. 2. Pull gently until the box starts to move. 3. Write down the reading, or how far the band stretched.
flow.say: First, let's measure how hard it is now, with nothing under the box.
flow.kid: Hook the forcemeter to the box. Pull until it moves. Write down the number.
flow.context: This is the first step of Move the Mountain. You measure how hard it is to move the heavy box before trying any tricks.

flow.do: Before trying anything, list three ideas together.
flow.say: Before we try anything, let's think like engineers. Let's list three ideas.
flow.kid: Think like an engineer! Draw or write three ideas to make it easier. Do this before you try any.

flow.do: 1. Try each idea one at a time. 2. Measure the pull for each. 3. Write each number down.
flow.say: Try one idea at a time and measure the pull. Which works best?
flow.kid: Try each idea, one at a time. Measure the pull each time. Which works best?
flow.parent: Round pencils used as rollers usually make a big difference. A cloth on tiles helps a little. Marbles under a tray can work very well. If the forcemeter reaches its last number, take one book out and start again from the first try, so every try uses the same load.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas together. Then invent a new one.
flow.say: Here is what engineers usually do, and some creative ideas. Can you invent something new?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ways, and some creative ideas. Now invent your own way. Can you beat them?
flow.think: Every wheel is a way of beating friction. Why do you think the wheel was such an important invention?

challenges.title: The Ghat Shoe
challenges.problem: A ghat is a row of wide stone steps going down to a river. When the steps are wet and mossy, people slip. Design a shoe or sandal sole that grips wet stone.
constraints: It must be cheap enough for anyone to buy.
It must be easy to take off at temple doors.
It must not scratch the old stone steps.
materials: paper, a pencil, rubber bands, an old chappal, and a wet patch of tiled floor for testing, such as the bathroom floor
general: Grooves that let water escape, so the rubber can touch the stone.
creative: Patterns copied from the toe pads of a tree frog or a gecko.
A wide, soft front to the sole, so more rubber touches the stone.
Strips of rough coir, the fibre from coconut husks.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your sole. Label each part with what it does. Then make a rubber-band version and test it on a wet tile.

flow.do: Collect a few different chappals and shoes. Turn them over and look at the bottoms together.
flow.say: What do the soles that grip best have in common?
flow.kid: Turn over different chappals and shoes. Look at the bottoms. What do the grippy ones have in common?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Ghat Shoe challenge. You look at real soles to see what makes some grip better than others.

flow.do: Explain the problem. On wet steps, water sits between the sole and the stone, like oil.
flow.say: Why are wet steps slippery? The water gets between the sole and the stone. It acts like oil.
flow.kid: Wet steps are slippery. Water sits between your sole and the stone, like oil. How could a sole push the water away?

check.q: Grooves in a sole help on wet steps because…
options: They let water escape, so the rubber can touch the stone
They make the shoe heavier, so it presses down more
check.why: On a wet step, a thin layer of water sits between the sole and the stone, like oil. The rubber can't grip through it. Grooves give the water somewhere to go. Then the rubber can touch the stone and grip.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws the sole and labels each part. 2. Wrap rubber bands tightly around an old chappal, as a test version. 3. Press it on a wet tile with your hand and push sideways. Feel how well it grips. Then do the same with a chappal that has no rubber bands. Which one grips better?
flow.say: Draw your sole and label what each part does. Then let's test a rubber-band version.
flow.kid: Draw your sole. Label each part. Then wrap rubber bands round an old chappal. Test it on a wet tile.

flow.do: Compare your design with the usual solutions and the creative ideas.
flow.say: Animals solved this long ago. Which animal would you copy?
flow.kid: Tree frogs climb wet leaves without slipping. Which animal's feet would you copy?
flow.think: Nature had millions of years to design feet. What else could we learn from it?

opts: Only on things that are moving fast
quiz.why: Friction needs two surfaces touching each other. Picking 'moving fast' usually means friction is linked only with speed. But it also holds still things in place. Magnets pull without touching, so that is a different force.

opts: The same way as the movement
quiz.why: Friction works against sliding. Picking 'the same way' often means friction is seen as a helper that carries things along. Picking 'downwards' mixes it up with gravity.

quiz.p: Which floor gives your feet the most grip?
opts: A shiny, polished floor that is wet
quiz.why: Rubber grips well. Picking the shiny floor often means shiny is thought of as clean and safe. Shiny, wet floors are actually slippery.

quiz.p: You test different shoes on the slope. To make it a fair test, what should change?
quiz.why: In a fair test, you change only one thing. Then you know that one thing caused the difference. Picking 'the shoe and the slope' usually means wanting to test more at once. Then you can't tell which change mattered.
quiz.context: In the slope test, you put a shoe on a board and lift one end until the shoe slides.

quiz.p: You pull two shoes across the floor with a forcemeter. Shoe A needs 3 newtons. Shoe B needs 6 newtons. Which has more friction?
quiz.why: Shoe B needed a bigger pull, 6 newtons instead of 3. So it has more friction. Picking A usually means a small number was read as a strong grip. Here, the number is how hard you had to pull, so bigger means more friction.
quiz.context: A forcemeter is a tool with a spring inside. It shows how hard you are pulling, in units called newtons.

quiz.p: Look at the bar chart of slope test heights. Which shoe has the tallest bar?
quiz.why: The tallest bar means that shoe stayed on the steepest slope. So it grips best. Picking 'slippery' often means the bar was read as 'how fast it slid'. The bar shows how high the board went before sliding.
quiz.context: In the slope test, you lift one end of a board until the shoe on it slides. Then you measure how high the end went.

chart.title: How high the board's end went before each one slid (made-up results)

quiz.p: Where do we want LESS friction?
quiz.why: A slide should be slippery, so you can whizz down it. Picking brakes or shoes means GRIP and SLIP got swapped. Those two need lots of friction.
Oil is a lubricant, a slippery layer that lowers friction. Picking sand often means tiny grains are pictured rolling like marbles. On ice, sand grains dig in and add grip.

quiz.p: Why do old temple steps have a dip in the middle?
opts: Friction from millions of feet wore them away
Heavy people squashed the stone down
quiz.why: Each footstep rubs off a tiny bit of stone. Over hundreds of years, this wear makes a dip. Picking 'squashed' usually means stone is pictured as soft, like clay. Hard stone does not squash. It wears away.

quiz.p: Rubbing your hands together makes them warm. Why?
opts: The air around you is warm
quiz.why: Friction turns the movement of your hands into heat. Picking 'blood rushes' is a sensible guess. But rub two sticks together and they warm up too, with no blood at all.

quiz.p: Do scientists fully know why ice is slippery?
opts: Yes, it is because pressure melts it
No, they are still studying it
Yes, it is because ice is always wet
quiz.why: Scientists still argue about it. Picking 'pressure melts it' means the old textbook idea has been met. Scientists now think that pressure is far too weak to explain it.

quiz.p: Who wrote down rules of friction first, but in notebooks that were never published?
quiz.why: Leonardo da Vinci wrote them around 1493. Amontons published them about 200 years later, in 1699. Picking Newton is a common guess, because he is famous for forces. But Newton was born more than 120 years after Leonardo died.

quiz.p: Deep down, where does friction come from?
opts: Atoms pushing and pulling with electric force
quiz.why: Friction comes from electric pushes and pulls between the atoms of the two surfaces. Picking 'tiny hooks' is close to the old bumps idea, which is part of the story. But even bumps grip through electric forces. Gravity is a different force.

quiz.p: Which of these flows with no friction at all?
opts: Superfluid helium, cooled to about 271 degrees below zero
quiz.why: Superfluid helium is so cold that it flows with zero friction. Picking water often means runny is taken to mean friction-free. Water flows easily, but it still has a little friction inside it.

quiz.p: Friction from the tides rubbing on the sea floor is…
opts: Pulling the Moon closer to us
quiz.why: Tidal friction slowly brakes Earth's spin. About 400 million years ago, a day lasted only about 22 hours. Picking 'Moon closer' is a natural guess, since the Moon's pull makes the tides. In fact the Moon is drifting away, about 3.8 centimetres a year.
quiz.context: Tides are the sea rising and falling, mostly because the Moon's gravity pulls on the water.

Pencils, chalk and crayons leave marks because rubbing wears a little of them off onto the paper.

Maglev trains, like the one in Shanghai, float above the track on magnets, so no wheels rub.
Air hockey tables and hovercraft ride on a cushion of air, with almost no rubbing.
Doctors fit new hip and knee joints that are made to slide with very little friction.
Superfluid helium, a liquid with no friction, helps cool the giant magnets of the Large Hadron Collider, a huge science machine in Europe.

open_questions.q: Exactly what happens between the atoms of two surfaces as they slide?
open_questions.why_open: It happens in spaces far too tiny to see. Scientists use special microscopes and computer models, and they still argue.
Several ideas compete. Maybe ice has a slippery layer on top. Maybe sliding melts a thin film. Maybe loose molecules on top roll like marbles.

open_questions.q: Can we make friction almost disappear?
open_questions.why_open: Some materials slide with almost no friction. One is graphene, a sheet of carbon just one atom thick, stacked in layers. Scientists call this superlubricity. So far it mostly works for very small pieces.

open_questions.q: Can we predict earthquakes by studying friction underground?
open_questions.why_open: Earthquakes happen when rocks that were stuck suddenly slip. How and when they slip is still too complicated to predict.

open_questions.q: How do gecko and frog feet grip so well, and let go so fast?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists understand parts of it. They keep copying it to make new sticky materials.

open_questions.q: Does 'quantum friction' really exist? It is a tiny drag predicted between surfaces that never touch.
open_questions.why_open: Some calculations predict it, others disagree, and nobody has measured it yet.

open_questions.q: Is friction's one-way nature the reason time only goes forwards?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists agree that things always spread from order into mess. Whether that is what makes time go forwards is still argued about.
Experiments show they do not simply add grip. They may help on wet surfaces, or mainly help us feel what we touch.

maths.problem: A shoe started to slide when the end of the board was 16 cm high. A sock slid when the end was only 8 cm high. Look at the chart. How many times higher was the shoe's height than the sock's?
maths.explain: The shoe stayed put until the end was 16 cm high. The sock slid at just 8 cm. 16 divided by 8 is 2. So the shoe's height was 2 times the sock's. You can check: 8 + 8 = 16.
maths.context: This is about the slope test. You put a shoe on a flat board and slowly lift one end. You measure how high the end is when the shoe starts to slide. The higher it goes first, the better the shoe grips.

maths.why_maths: Scientists don't just say 'the shoe grips better'. They ask 'how much better?' Dividing one number by the other tells us: this many times better.

maths.problem: Look at the forcemeter in the picture. The big numbers are whole newtons. Each small mark between them is half a newton. What is the reading?
maths.explain: The pointer is past the 4, but before the 5. It sits on the small mark exactly halfway between them. Each small mark is half a newton. So the reading is 4 newtons and half a newton more. That is 4 and a half newtons.
maths.context: A forcemeter is a tool with a spring inside that measures how hard you pull. As you pull, a pointer moves along a scale of numbers. The numbers are newtons, the units for pushes and pulls.

maths.why_maths: A forcemeter only helps if you can read it. Reading a scale with small marks between the numbers is the maths that turns a pointer into an answer.

maths.problem: Four shoes were tested. The board's end went this high before each one slid: rubber chappal 16 cm, school shoe 13 cm, sock 8 cm, slipper 11 cm. Draw a bar chart of these heights. Then answer: which one grips second best?
maths.answer: The school shoe grips second best. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each, as tall as its height. Then put the heights in order, from tallest to shortest: 16, 13, 11, 8. The tallest bar is the rubber chappal, at 16 cm. The next tallest is the school shoe, at 13 cm. So the school shoe grips second best.
maths.context: This is about the slope test. You put a shoe on a flat board and slowly lift one end. You measure how high the end is when the shoe starts to slide. The higher it goes first, the better the shoe grips.

answer_chart.title: How high the board's end went before each one slid

maths.why_maths: After a test you have a list of numbers, which is hard to compare at a glance. A bar chart turns the numbers into bars, so the best grip jumps out: the tallest bar wins.

maths.problem: Two notebooks have 40 pages each. You lay all their pages over each other, one from each book in turn. How many places are there where one page touches the next?
maths.explain: Altogether there are 40 + 40 = 80 pages in one pile. Between every two neighbouring pages there is one touching place. So there is always one fewer touching place than pages. 80 take away 1 is 79. Check with 3 pages: there are 2 touching places.
maths.context: In the Books That Won't Let Go experiment, you lay the pages of two notebooks over each other. You take one page from each book in turn. Every place where two pages touch adds a little friction.

answer_chart.title: Pages in the pile and places where pages touch

maths.why_maths: Friction adds up: every place where two pages touch adds a little grip. Counting those places, and spotting the pattern, shows why hundreds of pages are so hard to pull apart.

maths.problem: The Moon moves about 4 cm further from Earth every year. About how far will it move in 80 years, a long human lifetime? Give your answer in metres and centimetres.
maths.answer: About 320 cm, which is 3 metres and 20 centimetres.
maths.explain: Each year adds 4 cm. In 80 years, that is 80 lots of 4 cm. 4 × 80 = 320 cm. 100 cm make 1 metre, so 300 cm is 3 metres. That leaves 20 cm. So the answer is 3 metres and 20 centimetres. The real speed is a little less, about 3.8 cm a year. We rounded it to 4 cm to make the sum easier.
maths.context: The Moon is very slowly moving away from the Earth. This happens because friction from the sea's tides is slowing the Earth's spin.

answer_chart.title: How much further away the Moon moves, at about 4 cm a year

maths.why_maths: 4 cm a year sounds tiny. Multiplying it by the years of a whole life shows how small changes add up to something you could measure with your own arms.

roots.context: We have been learning about friction, the grip between things that touch. Now we ask what that grip tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: When you rub your palms fast and then stop, they are warm. Friction has turned their movement into the faster jiggling of countless tiny atoms. That warmth spreads into the air, and it never turns back into your hands moving. So when something stops, its movement has not ended, only spread out where we cannot see it.
deep_truth.habit: We say a moving thing 'stops', as if its movement simply ends. Friction shows that the movement is still there, only shared out among atoms where we cannot see it.
deep_truth.evidence: Rub your palms and they get warm. The warmth fades into the air, and it never turns back into your hands moving. A film of a box sliding to a stop looks wrong when it is played backwards.

three.who_am_i: When you rub your hands, the warmth you feel is your own movement, now shared with your skin and the air.
three.what_is_life: Living things control friction all the time. A gecko's feet grip a wall, and your knee joints stay slippery for a lifetime.
three.what_is_this_world: On Earth, every sliding thing slows down and warms what it rubs against. Even some of the Earth's spin is slowly being turned into warmth by the tides.

roots.thread: Friction does not destroy movement. It takes the neat movement of one thing and shares it out among countless atoms in the box, the floor and the air. DeepKids believes that everything comes from one whole and keeps flowing back into it. Friction is a small, everyday example: the movement of one thing becomes the warmth shared by many.

teachings.source: Isha Upanishad, opening verse (also Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 5.1.1)
teachings.teaching: That is whole, this is whole. From the whole the whole comes out. Take the whole from the whole, and the whole remains.
teachings.link: When friction stops a box, the box loses its movement, but the world loses no energy. The total stays the same, only spread out as warmth.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha taught that everything made of parts keeps changing. Nothing stays the same for ever.
teachings.link: Friction shows this slowly. Shoe soles, brake pads and stone temple steps wear away, and even the length of a day is changing because of the tides.

science.text: When friction stops a sliding box, its energy is not lost. It becomes the jiggling of atoms, which is heat. In the 1840s, James Joule showed that the same amount of stirring always makes the same amount of heat.
Many physicists think this one-way spreading is why time seems to go only forwards. Others say it explains which way things change, but not what time is.

other_view.view: Many physicists say there is nothing deeper here. There are far more messy ways for atoms to jiggle than neat ways, so things almost always end up spread out. To them, this is a matter of counting, not a sign of one whole.

practice.title: Warm hands
practice.say: Let's rub our palms together fast while I count to ten. Now stop and hold them still, a little apart. Feel the warmth in both palms. Close your eyes and just notice it fade. Where did the warmth come from? Where is it going now?
practice.kid: Rub your palms fast for ten seconds. Then hold them still. Feel the warmth. Notice it slowly fading away. Where is it going?

ask: When the warmth leaves your hands, is it gone, or somewhere else?
A ball rolls to a stop and warms the floor a tiny bit. Why does the warm floor never push the ball back?
If movement never ends but only spreads out, where is the movement of a ball you rolled yesterday?

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many scientists believed heat was an invisible fluid, called caloric. They thought every object held a certain amount of it. Rubbing, they said, only squeezed out caloric that was already inside. In 1798, Benjamin Thompson, known as Count Rumford, was in charge of making cannons in Munich, in Germany. Cannons were made by drilling a long hole into a solid block of metal. The drilling made the metal very hot. Rumford tried an experiment. He put a cannon in a box of cold water and turned a blunt drill inside it, using horses. After about two and a half hours, the water boiled. The people watching were amazed. As long as the horses kept turning, the heat kept coming. If heat were a fluid stored in the metal, it should have run out. So Rumford said heat must be a kind of movement instead. In the 1840s, James Joule measured how much heat a set amount of stirring makes. It was always the same, which showed that Rumford was right.
how_we_found_out.who: Benjamin Thompson (Count Rumford), and later James Joule
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Heat is an invisible fluid, called caloric, stored inside things. Rumford's blunt drill made heat for as long as the horses turned, so heat could not be a fluid that runs out.
